o: We must rotate a binary tree so that the leftmost path becomes the new spine. At each step along the original left-child chain, three rewirings happen: the left child becomes the parent, the old root becomes its right child, and the old right child becomes its left child. Because every right node has no children and always has a sibling, only nodes on the leftmost path ever have children — so we can walk down that single chain. For example 1: node 1 has left 2 (with children 4,5) and right 3; after flipping, 4 becomes root with right child 5 and left child 2, whose left child is 3 and right child is 1. Empty input returns null, and a single node is already its own flipped root. With at most 10 nodes, any traversal works, but an $O(n)$ iterative or recursive walk down the left spine is natural.
k: Only the leftmost path matters: every right subtree is a leaf, so flipping reduces to walking down left children.
At each node with left child L and right child R: new parent of current is L, current becomes L's right child, R becomes L's left child.
The new root is the leftmost (deepest-left) node of the original tree.

a.i: Recursively flip the left subtree first; when it returns, the deepest left node is the new root. On unwinding, rewire the current node: its left child's left pointer gets the current node's old right child, and its left child's right pointer gets the current node itself. Then detach the current node's own children to avoid cycles and return the saved new root upward.
s: If root is null or has no left child, return root (base case / new root).
Recurse on root.left to get newRoot.
Set root.left.left = root.right and root.left.right = root.
Clear root.left and root.right to null.

c.python:
# Definition for a binary tree node.
# class TreeNode:
#     def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.left = left
#         self.right = right
class Solution:
    def upsideDownBinaryTree(self, root):
        if not root or not root.left:
            return root
        new_root = self.upsideDownBinaryTree(root.left)
        root.left.left = root.right
        root.left.right = root
        root.left = None
        root.right = None
        return new_root

a.t: O(n) — each node on the left spine is visited once.
a.sp: O(h) recursion stack, where h is the height of the left spine (at most n).

a.i: Walk down the left spine while keeping pointers to the previous node, its previous right sibling, and the current node. At each step, save the next left child, then attach: current's left becomes prevRight, current's right becomes prev, and advance. This avoids recursion entirely and produces the same result in one pass.
s: Initialize cur = root, prev = null, prevRight = null.
While cur exists: save next = cur.left.
Set cur.left = prevRight and cur.right = prev.
Advance: prevRight = cur.right was just overwritten, so instead track: prevRight = old cur.right before overwrite; simpler: store tmp = cur.right before rewiring.
Move prev = cur, cur = next; finally return prev (the last node reached).

c.python:
class Solution:
    def upsideDownBinaryTree(self, root):
        cur, prev, prev_right = root, None, None
        while cur:
            nxt = cur.left
            tmp = cur.right
            cur.left = prev_right
            cur.right = prev
            prev_right = tmp
            prev = cur
            cur = nxt
        return prev

a.t: O(n) — one pass along the left spine.
a.sp: O(1) — only a constant number of pointer variables.

w: In an interview, start with the recursive version since it maps directly onto the problem description, then mention the O(1)-space iterative version as the optimal follow-up. Common pitfalls: forgetting to null out the original root's children in the recursive solution (creating cycles), mishandling empty trees and single-node trees, and overwriting cur.right before saving it in the iterative loop. Edge cases: null root, one node, a straight left chain with no right children. Likely follow-ups: do it iteratively with O(1) space, handle trees where right nodes may have children (the guarantee would need revisiting), or flip back to restore the original tree.
